extracted.intended_audience: math olympiad contestants, coaches, and problem-solvers reading China Mathematical Olympiad problems and solutions
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques, proof-strategies, and constructive/counterexample requirements used when solving/justifying solutions to Olympiad-style problems (geometry, combinatorics, number theory, inequalities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the Pigeonhole Principle for existence arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the Pigeon Hole Principle to force multiplicities/placements of points or objects (e.g., to show there exist at least 3 points on one side of a line or to deduce a sector receives frogs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the text: "By the Pigeon Hole Principle, there exist at least 3 points on one side of line P1P2," and similarly used to find multiple points in one area/sector. Use this to extract a smaller configuration (e.g., a convex pentagon) with additional properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal counterexample / least-area argument using integrality of area
rubrics_metrics.description: When assuming a counterexample exists, choose one of minimal area (or minimal discrete measure) and derive a contradiction using integrality/discreteness properties of area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original guidance: "Then among such pentagons there must be one, denoted by ABCDE, which has the least area, since the value of the area of a polygon with integral vertices is always in the form of 1/2 (n ∈ N)." Use midpoint/integral-lattice arguments to reduce area and contradict minimality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity/classification on lattice points to produce integral midpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify integer-coordinate points according to parity of coordinates (odd/even combinations) to force two vertices to share parity and hence have an integral midpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "There are only 4 cases concerning the odd/even property of the xy-coordinate of an integral point: (odd, even), (even, odd), (odd, odd), (even, even). So there must be two vertices ... the midpoint ... is also an integral point." Use this to produce additional lattice points lying on edges or inside polygons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct explicit configuration to show attainability of minimal bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a claimed minimal n (or minimal/count bound) is attainable, provide a concrete construction/configuration and verify it satisfies the required conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to show n=11 is attainable, the solution gives an explicit set M of integer points (vertices and four interior points) and then verifies condition (2) by contradiction/case analysis. Always accompany constructions with a full check that they meet the problem constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence via odd-degree polynomial root (intermediate-value style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model a parameter (e.g., x1) so that the target condition becomes a real polynomial equation in that parameter; if the polynomial degree is odd, there is guaranteed a real root.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "x_{n+1} is a polynomial of x1 with degree 3^n and real coefficients. As 3^n is an odd number, there exists a real number x1 such that x_{n+1}=0." Use degree-parity and continuity/Intermediate Value considerations to conclude existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness via maximal-difference contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove uniqueness of a constructed sequence/solution, assume two solutions exist; consider an index where their difference is maximal and derive a contradiction (often by bounding propagated differences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From text: set up recurrence for differences and suppose |w_i - v_i| is greatest; show it must be zero or lead to contradiction. This maximal-difference method is standard for uniqueness proofs in recurrence problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply standard inequalities (Cauchy, Jensen, Bernoulli, mean inequality, binomial formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use classical inequalities as appropriate to derive bounds, monotonicity, or to simplify expressions (frequent in inequality problems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances: "Using the Cauchy Inequality...", "By using Bernoulli's inequality...", "By the mean inequality...", and use of the binomial formula to estimate terms. Also: define concave functions and apply Jensen (see f(x)=ln(...)). Combine inequalities where needed (e.g., Jensen + Cauchy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define invariants/equilibrium and monovariants (potential functions) in combinatorial dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: For processes/dynamics (e.g., frogs jumping), define an invariant/equilibrium property and/or a potential (monovariant) function that strictly changes under allowed moves; use boundedness of potential to force certain events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text example: define a grid to be 'in equilibrium' if it or all three neighbors have frogs; show equilibrium persists and that a sum-of-squares labeling potential increases by 2 on certain moves but cannot increase indefinitely, forcing frogs into a sector. This method proves eventual uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Ceva's theorem / sine rule / ratio chasing for concurrency
rubrics_metrics.description: In geometry concurrency problems, compute directed ratios or products of sines/lengths and apply (the inverse of) Ceva's theorem combined with the sine rule to prove lines are concurrent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: apply sine rule to many small triangles to obtain equal ratios, multiply relations and use inverse Ceva: "Finally, according to the inverse of Ceva's Theorem, we know AL, BM and CN have a common point."

rubrics_metrics.name: Partition/area-counting and case-splitting to obtain minimal counts (combinatorial geometry)
rubrics_metrics.description: To lower-bound counts of sub-configurations (e.g., triangles of small area among points), partition the region (midpoint lines, small rectangles), apply pigeonhole, then perform case analysis on the convex hull (triangle/quad/pentagon) to count 'good' triples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example method: divide rectangle into 4 small rectangles via midpoints; ensure at least two points in one small rectangle; distinguish cases for location of other points and use area inequalities to show at least two good triples; provide constructions where lower bound is tight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diophantine/exponential equations: use modular arithmetic and parity constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze exponentiation equations by reducing modulo small bases (2,3,4,5,7,8,9,16,...), determine parity and congruence classes of exponents to restrict possibilities, combine with small-case checking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text repeatedly uses: deduce exponents odd/even via mod arguments, eliminate possibilities, and perform direct computation for small exponents. Use congruence contradictions to show impossibility or to identify all solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use induction with explicit constructive recurrence for existence of partitions/representations
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving existence of representations (e.g., representing large n as sum of r integers with monotonic constraints), prove base case and use an inductive construction with an explicit bound/function N(r) to extend to larger r.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for any r>2 there exists N(r) such that every n>N(r) admits required representation; inductive step sets N(K+1)=4N(K)^3 and constructs representations by splitting n appropriately. Provide base values and constructive steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concavity and Jensen's inequality to bound sums of nonlinear functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Define an appropriate concave function f and apply Jensen to bound averages/sums, often in combination with Cauchy to obtain desired inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From text: define f(x)=ln((1+x)/(1-x)) (or similar), show f is concave, apply Jensen to obtain f(x1)+...+f(xn) ≥ n f(average), combine with other inequalities to conclude the target bound.
